name: TgCrypto (pyrogram/tgcrypto)
workload: No benchmark found: the README, the repository, the commit titles, the issue tracker and README revisions 95ff73c (v1.1.1), d6fbe3c (v1.0.2) and 5c2c7f3 contain no timing numbers and no OpenSSL comparison.
claimed_speedup: No numeric claim found. README says only 'designed to be portable, fast, easy to install and use' and 'Fast and Portable Cryptography Extension Library for Pyrogram'. The orchestrator's lead (41 vs 23 MB/s at 48-byte messages versus OpenSSL-based IGE) could not be located in any opened source.
stars_or_usage: 211 stars; archived by owner 2024-12-23; Pyrogram's optional accelerator (PyPI TgCrypto, fork pyrotgcrypto)
tradeoffs: Python C extension implementing AES-256-IGE (MTProto 2.0), AES-256-CTR and AES-256-CBC only. Inputs must be padded to a multiple of 16 bytes by the caller. Portable table-based AES (Te0/Td0 lookup tables in aes256.c, no AES-NI, ARM Crypto or other intrinsics found in the source), so it is not constant-time against cache attacks. README states the algorithm implementations are 'for educational purposes only'. Releases the GIL (commit 'Released the GIL', 2019-06-13).
caveats: No evidence that it beats OpenSSL. Lead not substantiated: no benchmark in README (checked current README and revisions 95ff73c, d6fbe3c, 5c2c7f3), commit titles, issues (search returned 0 results) or source comments. The source is a portable T-table AES, so beating OpenSSL's AES-NI based core on large buffers is implausible; only per-call overhead on tiny messages measured through Python could favour it, and no such measurement was found. Third-party package aesige (Apache-2.0, AES-NI / ARM Crypto Extensions, https://pypi.org/project/aesige/ page opened via the PyPI JSON API) reports tgcrypto at 14.8 us decrypt and 24.3 us encrypt for 1 KB versus 7.4 us and 7.7 us for aesige on x86_64, i.e. tgcrypto is 2-3.2x slower than a hardware-accelerated IGE (author's own numbers, no CPU stated). Archived and unmaintained since 2024-12-23. LGPL licence: the sidebar also lists GPL-3.0 text; README says LGPLv3+. Pyrogram docs and Telethon cryptg pages were not reachable here.

name: SHA-Intrinsics (noloader)
baseline: portable C SHA-256 (the repo's own sha256.c reference) and OpenSSL SHA-256: neither is measured in the README
workload: README reports Botan 'speed --msec=3000' hashing of 1024-byte buffers (SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512) with Botan using these SHA-NI / ARMv8 / Power8 compression functions; there is no baseline column.
claimed_speedup: No speedup stated; the README says 'The speedups can be tricky to measure' and lists only absolute Botan numbers. Intel SHA on Celeron J3455: SHA-256 445.747 MiB/sec at 3.64 cycles/byte (GCC 7.3.1) and 447.657 MiB/sec at 3.62 cycles/byte (Clang 5.0.1); SHA-1 889.903 MiB/sec at 1.82 cycles/byte (GCC 7.3.1). ARMv8 (Kirin 620, Cortex-A53 1.2 GHz, GCC 4.9.2): SHA-256 599.463 MiB/sec. The same Intel run shows SHA-512 (no SHA-512 hardware) at 121.721 MiB/sec and 13.32 cycles/byte, but that is a different algorithm so no ratio is derived. Power8 built-ins: SHA-256 250.424 MiB/sec at 12.95 cycles/byte, which the README calls 'not that impressive'.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.3.1 and Clang 5.0.1 (x86); GCC 4.9.2 (ARM); GCC 7.2.0 (POWER8). README build flags: -msse4 -msha (x86), -march=armv8-a+crc+crypto (ARM), -mcpu=power8 (POWER8). Botan's own build flags are not stated.
hardware: Intel Celeron J3455 1.5 GHz (burst 2.2 GHz), ASUS J3455M-E; Kirin 620 octa-core Cortex-A53 1.2 GHz (README also names an ARMv8 LeMaker HiKey); ppc64le POWER8 3.4 GHz (GCC112, compile farm)
stars_or_usage: 232 stars; README benchmarks are Botan runs that use this code
tradeoffs: Only the SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256 and SHA-512 compression functions on full blocks: the caller sets the initial state and pads the final block, and the sample main hashes an empty message only. Needs SHA-NI (x86 -msha), ARMv8 crypto extensions or POWER8; Power8 gain is flat. No runtime CPU dispatch in the code (cpuid.c is a sample).
caveats: No baseline measured: the README gives no portable-C or OpenSSL row, and the numbers come from Botan using this code, not from the repo's own harness. No LICENSE file (raw LICENSE returns 404); each source file header says 'Written and placed in public domain by Jeffrey Walton' (no patent grant). The x86 files are 'based on code from Intel, and by Sean Gulley for the miTLS project' and the ARM files on ARM and mbedTLS code, so the public-domain dedication of derived code is unverified. Last commit 2026-01-08 is a merge of PR #14 and its revert; the last substantive change is 2024-02-24 ('ARM: fix incorrect variable names'), so the repo is effectively finished. Clang 3.7 ARM results are 'To be determined'.

name: isa-l_crypto multi-buffer SHA-256 (sha256_mb)
baseline: single-buffer SHA-256: Rust sha2 crate (serial, hardware-accelerated) in the only numeric comparison found; the repo's own perf test targets OpenSSL SHA256() but publishes no numbers
workload: Third-party harness (tape-sha256 merkle_leaves bench): one Solana erasure batch of 64 independent messages, each a 26-byte prefix plus about 1 KiB payload (67,680 bytes per batch), one thread pinned to one physical core, best of 15 rounds of 50 iterations; isa-l_crypto built from source on the test machine.
claimed_speedup: AMD Zen 5 (same-session): isa-l_crypto avx512-16 10.92 us/batch (6195 MB/s), avx512-ni-16 10.85 us (6237 MB/s), dispatched 10.89 us (6213 MB/s) versus sha2 serial 27.71 us/batch (2443 MB/s), about 2.5x (derived from page data). The benchmark author's own tape-sha256 avx512-2x16 (7.82 us) was 39% faster than the best isa-l_crypto result in that run. Intel's Multi-Hash white paper (in the repo wiki) separately claims about 5 cycles/byte for Multi-Hash SHA-256 on a Core i7-2600, 'over 2X faster than the best known SHA-256 single buffer implementations' (different construction, mh_sha256).
compiler_and_flags: isa-l_crypto 'built from source on the machine being tested'; compiler and flags not stated (NASM assembly plus C); harness is Rust 1.89+ via cargo bench
hardware: AMD family 0x1a (Zen 5), exact processor model not captured, measured 2026-08-08
tradeoffs: Multi-buffer hashing only helps when many independent messages are available: the sha256_mb context manager (submit / flush jobs) interleaves up to 4/8/16 messages across SSE, AVX, AVX2 or AVX-512 lanes, with SHA-NI single-stream kernels (sha256_ni_x1/x2) for small batches. A single message gets no speedup; very short or unevenly sized messages lose lanes to padding. Also provides sha1_mb, sha512_mb, md5_mb, sm3_mb, mh_sha1/mh_sha256 multi-hash (changes the digest: not plain SHA-256), AES-XTS/GCM/CBC and rolling hash. x86 NASM-based and aarch64.
caveats: Numbers come from a competitor's benchmark in the tape-sha256 crate (BENCHMARKS.md inside the crates.io tarball; the GitHub repo spool-labs/tape-sha256 returns 404), so the harness is only reachable as a crate tarball; the baseline is the Rust sha2 crate, not OpenSSL. The repo itself ships sha256_mb/sha256_mb_vs_ossl_perf.c (32 buffers of 4 KiB, 4000 loops, OpenSSL SHA256() against isal_sha256_ctx_mgr_submit/flush, plus a _cold variant) but README, wiki (empty 'TBD'), and Release_notes.txt carry no numbers. Intel's Xeon Scalable cryptographic performance article reportedly lists multi-buffer SHA-256 at 2.60 cycles/byte (AVX2 Xeon V4) and 0.87 (AVX-512) from search-result snippets only; the page itself is not reachable here. Only one CPU (Zen 5, model not captured) has an isa-l_crypto row in the tape-sha256 benchmark. Multi-buffer needs independent messages, so it is not a drop-in single-stream OpenSSL replacement.

name: Firedancer fd_sha256 batch (AVX-512 / AVX2 / SHA-NI)
baseline: single-buffer SHA-256: Rust sha2 crate (serial, hardware-accelerated) in the only numeric comparison found; no OpenSSL comparison found
workload: Third-party harness (tape-sha256 merkle_leaves bench): one Solana erasure batch of 64 independent messages, each a 26-byte prefix plus about 1 KiB payload (67,680 bytes per batch), one thread pinned to one physical core, best of 15 rounds of 50 iterations; the Firedancer harness builds prefix||leaf outside the timed region. Firedancer built from source on the test machine.
claimed_speedup: Versus sha2 serial, same session (ratios derived from page data): AMD Zen 5 avx512-16 12.55 us/batch (5393 MB/s) vs 27.71 us (2443 MB/s), about 2.2x; AMD Zen 4 EPYC 9B14 avx512-16 22.51 us (3006 MB/s) vs 43.71 us (1548 MB/s), about 1.9x; Xeon Platinum 8581C avx512-16 21.82 us (3102 MB/s) vs 49.18 us (1376 MB/s), about 2.25x; Xeon 6985P-C avx512-16 16.89 us (4006 MB/s) vs 36.87 us (1835 MB/s), about 2.2x. Not faster on AMD Zen 3 EPYC 7B13: avx-8 45.87 us (1476 MB/s) vs sha2 42.66 us (1587 MB/s), about 0.93x. The crate author's tape-sha256 beat Firedancer by 60% on Zen 5 but was 2-12% slower on the Intel parts.
compiler_and_flags: Firedancer 'built from source on the machine being tested' with a machine profile that exports the AVX-512 symbol (e.g. build/linux/gcc/zen5); compiler version and flags otherwise not stated
hardware: AMD Zen 5 (family 0x1a, model not captured); EPYC 9B14 (GCP c3d); EPYC 7B13 (GCP c2d); Xeon Platinum 8581C (GCP c4); Xeon 6985P-C (GCP c4-standard-8-lssd)
tradeoffs: src/ballet/sha256 has fd_sha256_batch_avx.c (8 lanes) and fd_sha256_batch_avx512.c (16 lanes) for independent messages, plus fd_sha256_hash_32_repeated_batch for PoH-style chains; the batch API needs contiguous messages and falls back to SHA-NI or scalar for small batches. Depends on Firedancer's util headers (fd_util, simd/fd_avx512.h), so extraction means vendoring part of the tree. The scalar core fd_sha256_core_ref is derived from OpenSSL's OPENSSL_SMALL_FOOTPRINT SHA-256 (Apache-2.0).
caveats: The repo itself carries no baseline numbers: test_sha256.c --bench prints only Gbps 'Ethernet equiv throughput / core' for incremental, streamlined and batched modes (14 and 1472 byte payloads) with no OpenSSL row, and header comments give no ratios. The only comparison is from the rival tape-sha256 crate (BENCHMARKS.md inside the crates.io tarball; its GitHub repo spool-labs/tape-sha256 returns 404), against the Rust sha2 crate rather than OpenSSL, and with Firedancer built by the benchmark author, who competes with it. Batch hashing needs independent messages. Zen 5 CPU model not captured; compiler flags not stated. Zen 3 and Zen 4 rows show the AVX-512 or AVX path is not always faster than serial SHA-NI.

name: fiat-crypto (generated Curve25519 field arithmetic in BoringSSL)
language: Coq (generates C, Rust, Go, Java, Zig, Bedrock2, x86-64 asm)
baseline: BoringSSL's previous curve25519 code: hand-written x86_64 x25519 assembly (884086e) and the earlier C field arithmetic on master (b2c312d)
workload: bssl speed -filter 25519 in BoringSSL: Curve25519 base-point multiplication, arbitrary-point multiplication, Ed25519 sign / verify ops/sec, with fiat-crypto generated 64-bit (fiat64) and 32-bit field code swapped in.
claimed_speedup: No field-level speedup: parity or slightly slower. BoringSSL commit 884086e ('Remove x86_64 x25519 assembly'): assembly 15095.3 ops/sec base-point and 15094.0 ops/sec arbitrary-point versus fiat64 38817.1 and 13905.1 ops/sec; message says 'The assembly is still about 9% faster than fiat64' on arbitrary-point multiplication; fiat64 wins base-point multiplication (about 2.6x, derived from page data) only because it can use the Ed25519 tables (at the cost of touching a 30kB table); the commit's own combined figure goes from 7547 to 10237 ops/sec. Commit b2c312d (fiat-crypto field arithmetic): per the page, branch 3546.5 / 3530.2 / 3014.5 ops/sec arbitrary-point and 11061.4 / 11226.2 / 8599.2 base-point versus master 3549.0 and 11177.1, i.e. parity.
compiler_and_flags: clang / clang++ with CMake and Ninja, Release build (commit b2c312d); 884086e states no toolchain
hardware: Google Cloud 'unidentified Intel Xeon with AVX2' (commit b2c312d); 884086e states no CPU
stars_or_usage: 844 stars; generated code adopted in BoringSSL (commits b2c312d, 884086e) and, per Linux commit 0ed42a6f431e, the kernel's 32-bit Curve25519
tradeoffs: Coq-verified synthesis of word-by-word field arithmetic (Curve25519 5x51-bit and 10x25.5-bit limbs, P-256, secp256k1, 80+ primes); the product is generated straight-line C (fiat-c), Rust, Go, Java, Zig, Bedrock2 and some amd64 asm, with proofs of the arithmetic but not of the C-to-machine step. Only field arithmetic: scalar-multiplication ladders, tables and protocols come from the host library. Generated code is large and unidiomatic.
caveats: Evidence supports 'as fast as hand-written C, correct by construction', not 'faster'. Measurements are by BoringSSL's maintainer on one unidentified Xeon with AVX2, so CPU model is missing (tier B, not A); the 884086e commit states no hardware or compiler. The b2c312d table was read from the GitHub page through a summarizing fetch tool, not verbatim. The IEEE S&P 2019 paper (Erbsen et al.) and Jason Gross' thesis, which compare against hand-written C and OpenSSL, were not reachable (dspace.mit.edu, wireguard.com, ieee-security.org, adam.chlipala.net blocked here); search snippets only say 'competitive performance for 80 prime fields' and 'first verified high-performance P-256', with no numbers. Linux kernel commit 0ed42a6f431e calls the Fiat 32-bit and HACL* 64-bit code 'the fastest available C implementations' without numbers. The repo README, boringssl_notes.md and folkwisdom.md contain no benchmark tables. Not OpenSSL itself: the baseline is BoringSSL's earlier curve25519 code.

name: tape-sha256
baseline: sha2 crate (serial SHA-256); also OpenSSL SHA-256 via Node.js node:crypto, and C batch hashers Firedancer fd_sha256 and isa-l_crypto sha256_mb
workload: Batch of 64 independent messages (26-byte prefix plus about 1 KiB payload, 67,680 bytes per batch, one Solana erasure batch of Merkle leaves), one thread pinned to one core, best of 15 rounds of 50 iterations; also hash chains in ns per link and Merkle commitments.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md summary vs sha2: AMD Zen 5 3.5x (avx512-2x16), Zen 4 2.1x (shani-x4), Zen 3 2.1x, Intel Emerald / Granite Rapids 2.0-2.1x, Apple M-series 6.8x; Zen 5 7.82 us/batch (8654 MB/s) vs sha2 27.71 us (2443 MB/s). Versus C implementations: 60% faster than Firedancer and 39% faster than the best isa-l_crypto result on Zen 5, about 8% faster than Firedancer on Zen 4, about 2.2x on Zen 3, but 2-12% slower than Firedancer on Intel Emerald Rapids / Granite Rapids in measured runs. Hash chains: 7.3 ns/link at 32 chains vs sha2 45.4 ns on Zen 5 (6.0x). OpenSSL: benches/wasm/README.md says the native neon-sha2-x4 batch (about 16 us; BENCHMARKS.md lists 16.25 us) is 2.7x faster than node:crypto (OpenSSL), whose crypto.hash one-shot took 42.89 us/batch (1578 MB/s) on an M4 Max (unpinned, read as ratios).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.89+ (rust-version) cargo bench, release profile; RUSTFLAGS not stated for native rows (notes that -C target-cpu=native made the Zen 5 interlaced kernel 8-14% slower); wasm rows built with -C target-feature=+simd128; Firedancer and isa-l_crypto built from source with unstated flags
hardware: AMD Zen 5 (family 0x1a, model not captured, 2026-08-08); EPYC 9B14 (GCP c3d); EPYC 7B13 (GCP c2d); Xeon Platinum 8581C (GCP c4); Xeon 6985P-C (GCP c4-standard-8-lssd); Apple M-series (M4 Max per the wasm README)
stars_or_usage: crates.io: 470 downloads, versions 0.1.0 (2026-07-27) and 0.2.1 (2026-08-11); GitHub repo returns 404
tradeoffs: Pure Rust (stable, no C dependency) multi-buffer SHA-256: hash_many, hash_many_prefixed, hash_pairs for independent messages (SIMD lane per message) and hash_chain / hash_chains for iterated 32-byte hashing (Solana proof-of-history). Runtime dispatch over AVX-512, AVX2, SHA-NI, ARM SHA-2, NEON, WebAssembly simd128 and portable fallbacks. No streaming single-message API, so a single large message gets no speedup; pre-1.0. WebCrypto beats the wasm build for batched ~1 KB messages in Chrome.
caveats: The GitHub repository named in the crates.io repository field (https://github.com/spool-labs/tape-sha256) returns HTTP 404, so it is private or removed; code, benches and BENCHMARKS.md were read from the crates.io 0.2.1 tarball (last_commit unknown: .cargo_vcs_info.json records git sha 5e72f679f750fe9e7fe166ae832003739e868e14). First-party measurements by the author, and the main baseline is the Rust sha2 crate, not OpenSSL; the only OpenSSL comparison is through Node.js (call overhead included, M4 Max unpinned, native batch number from a different document than the node:crypto number, so cross-run). Benchmarks are same-machine paired but compiler flags and several CPU models (Zen 5, Apple) are not captured. Does not win everywhere: 2-12% slower than Firedancer on Intel Emerald / Granite Rapids; the Firedancer harness builds prefix||leaf outside the timed region while tape reads prefix and body from separate slices. Results are single-core batch hashing, not application speedups (the README also cites 14-21% faster Agave shred recovery, unverified). Tests cross-check every backend against the sha2 crate.
